messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: Times in the app are rendered by the server, in the server's timezone. That's
wrong for anyone anywhere else, and it kills page caching: everyone's clock
ends up baked into HTML we'd like to share between people.

Move time rendering into the browser, everywhere we show a date or time. The
server sends the raw timestamp; the page turns it into words in the viewer's
own timezone. A comment from two hours ago reads "1:42 PM"; one from last
night reads "yesterday"; one from earlier in the week reads "5 days ago" or
"Sep 12"; a card auto-closing overnight reads "tomorrow", further out "in 3
days".

{

  "output_head": "# Fizzy

Guidance for AI coding agents working with this repository.

Fizzy is a kanban-style project management and issue tracker: cards move across columns on boards, with comments, mentions, and assignments.

## Deploy

Default branch: `main`

Self-hosted deploys run Kamal against `config/deploy.yml` — see `docs/kamal-deployment.md`.

## SaaS mode

For local agent work, `tmp/saas.txt` is the checkout-level SaaS switch used by `bin/setup`. When present, read `saas/AGENTS.md` before continuing. Otherwise, do not apply its instructions.

## Architecture Overview

### Multi-Tenancy (URL-Based)

Fizzy uses **URL path-based multi-tenancy**:
- Accounts have a unique decimal `external_account_id` used in URL prefixes
- URLs are prefixed: `/{account_id}/boards/...`
- Middleware (`AccountSlug::Extractor`) extracts the account ID from the URL and sets `Current.account`
- The slug is moved from `PATH_INFO` to `SCRIPT_NAME`, making Rails think it's "mounted" at that path
- Tenant-scoped domain records are account-isolated; global identity, session, and authentication records are exceptions
- Background jobs automatically serialize and restore account context

**Key insight**: This architecture allows multi-tenancy without subdomains or separate databases, making local development and testing simpler.

### Authentication & Authorization

Passwordless magic link authentication. A global `Identity` (email-based) can have `Users` in multiple Accounts, so an email is not a single account membership. Users have roles: owner, admin, member, system. Board-level access control via `Access` records.

### Entropy System

Cards automatically "postpone" (move to "not now") after inactivity:
- Account-level default entropy period
- Board-level entropy override
- Prevents endless todo lists from accumulating
- Configurable via Account/Board settings

### UUID Primary Keys

All tables use UUIDs (UUIDv7 format, base36-encoded as 25-char strings):
- Custom fixture UUID generation maintains deterministic ordering for tests
- Fixtures are always "older" than runtime records
- `.first`/`.last` work correctly in tests

### Background Jobs (Solid Queue)

Database-backed job queue (no Redis):
- Custom `FizzyActiveJobExtensions` prepended to ActiveJob
- Jobs automatically capture/restore `Current.account`
- Mission Control::Jobs for monitoring

Recurring tasks are declared in `config/recurring.yml`.

### Sharded Full-Text Search

Full-text search runs in the database, not Elasticsearch. On MySQL it is sharded 16 ways by CRC32 of the account ID (`Search::Record::Trilogy`); on SQLite it is a single FTS5 index (`Search::Record::SQLite`). Don't assume the sharded shape when working under SQLite. Models in `app/models/search/`.

### Imports and exports

Allow people to move between OSS and SAAS Fizzy instances:
- Exports/Imports can be written to/read from local or S3 storage depending on the config of the instance (both must be supported)
- Must be able to handle very large ZIP files (500+GB)
- Models in `app/models/account/data_transfer/`, `app/models/zip_file`

## Coding style

Before editing or reviewing code, read STYLE.md.
=== STYLE.md ===

# Style

We aim to write code that is a pleasure to read, and we have a lot of opinions about how to do it well. Writing great code is an essential part of our programming culture, and we deliberately set a high bar for every code change anyone contributes. We care about how code reads, how code looks, and how code makes you feel when you read it.

We love discussing code. If you have questions about how to write something, or if you detect some smell you are not quite sure how to solve, please ask away to other programmers. A Pull Request is a great way to do this.

When writing new code, unless you are very familiar with our approach, try to find similar code elsewhere to look for inspiration.

## Conditional returns

In general, we prefer to use expanded conditionals over guard clauses.

```ruby
# Bad
def todos_for_new_group
  ids = params.require(:todolist)[:todo_ids]
  return [] unless ids
  @bucket.recordings.todos.find(ids.split(","))
end

# Good
def todos_for_new_group
  if ids = params.require(:todolist)[:todo_ids]
    @bucket.recordings.todos.find(ids.split(","))
  else
    []
  end
end
```

This is because guard clauses can be hard to read, especially when they are nested.

As an exception, we sometimes use guard clauses to return early from a method:

* When the return is right at the beginning of the method.
* When the main method body is not trivial and involves several lines of code.

```ruby
def after_recorded_as_commit(recording)
  return if recording.parent.was_created?

  if recording.was_created?
    broadcast_new_column(recording)
  else
    broadcast_column_change(recording)
  end
end
```

## Methods ordering

We order methods in classes in the following order:

1. `class` methods
2. `public` methods with `initialize` at the top.
3. `private` methods

## Invocation order

We order m",
  "output_tail": "difiers, and we indent the content under them.

```ruby
class SomeClass
  def some_method
    # ...
  end

  private
    def some_private_method_1
      # ...
    end

    def some_private_method_2
      # ...
    end
end
```

If a module only has private methods, we mark it `private` at the top and add an extra new line after but don't indent.

```ruby
module SomeModule
  private
  
  def some_private_method
    # ...
  end
end
```

## CRUD controllers

We model web endpoints as CRUD operations on resources (REST). When an action doesn't map cleanly to a standard CRUD verb, we introduce a new resource rather than adding custom actions.

```ruby
# Bad
resources :cards do
  post :close
  post :reopen
end

# Good
resources :cards do
  resource :closure
end
```

## Controller and model interactions

In general, we favor a [vanilla Rails](https://dev.37signals.com/vanilla-rails-is-plenty/) approach with thin controllers directly invoking a rich domain model. We don't use services or other artifacts to connect the two.

Invoking plain Active Record operations is totally fine:

```ruby
class Cards::CommentsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @comment = @card.comments.create!(comment_params)
  end
end
```

For more complex behavior, we prefer clear, intention-revealing model APIs that controllers call directly:

```ruby
class Cards::GoldnessesController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @card.gild
  end
end
```

When justified, it is fine to use services or form objects, but don't treat those as special artifacts:

```ruby
Signup.new(email_address: email_address).create_identity
```

## Run async operations in jobs

As a general rule, we write shallow job classes that delegate the logic itself to domain models:

* We typically use the suffix `_later` to flag methods that enqueue a job.
* A common scenario is having a model class that enqueues a job that, when executed, invokes some method in that same class. In this case, we use the suffix `_now` for the regular synchronous method.

```ruby
module Event::Relaying
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    after_create_commit :relay_later
  end

  def relay_later
    Event::RelayJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  def relay_now
    # ...
  end
end

class Event::RelayJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(event)
    event.relay_now
  end
end
```

* When the main method body is not trivial and involves several lines of code.

```ruby
def after_recorded_as_commit(recording)
  return if recording.parent.was_created?

  if recording.was_created?
    broadcast_new_column(recording)
  else
    broadcast_column_change(recording)
  end
end
```

## Methods ordering

We order methods in classes in the following order:

1. `class` methods
2. `public` methods with `initialize` at the top.
3. `private` methods

## Invocation order

We order m
...[882 characters omitted]...
difiers, and we indent the content under them.

```ruby
class SomeClass
  def some_method
    # ...
  end

  private
    def some_private_method_1
      # ...
    end

    def some_private_method_2
      # ...
    end
end
```

If a module only has private methods, we mark it `private` at the top and add an extra new line after but don't indent.

```ruby
module SomeModule
  private
  
  def some_private_method
    # ...
  end
end
```

## CRUD controllers

We model web endpoints as CRUD operations on resources (REST). When an action doesn't map cleanly to a standard CRUD verb, we introduce a new resource rather than adding custom actions.

```ruby
# Bad
resources :cards do
  post :close
  post :reopen
end

# Good
resources :cards do
  resource :closure
end
```

## Controller and model interactions

In general, we favor a [vanilla Rails](https://dev.37signals.com/vanilla-rails-is-plenty/) approach with thin controllers directly invoking a rich domain model. We don't use services or other artifacts to connect the two.

Invoking plain Active Record operations is totally fine:

```ruby
class Cards::CommentsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @comment = @card.comments.create!(comment_params)
  end
end
```

For more complex behavior, we prefer clear, intention-revealing model APIs that controllers call directly:

```ruby
class Cards::GoldnessesController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @card.gild
  end
end
```

When justified, it is fine to use services or form objects, but don't treat those as special artifacts:

```ruby
Signup.new(email_address: email_address).create_identity
```

## Run async operations in jobs

As a general rule, we write shallow job classes that delegate the logic itself to domain models:

* We typically use the suffix `_later` to flag methods that enqueue a job.
* A common scenario is having a model class that enqueues a job that, when executed, invokes some method in that same class. In this case, we use the suffix `_now` for the regular synchronous method.

```ruby
module Event::Relaying
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    after_create_commit :relay_later
  end

  def relay_later
    Event::RelayJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  def relay_now
    # ...
  end
end

class Event::RelayJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(event)
    event.relay_now
  end
end
```

Okay, here's the breakdown of my thought process after seeing those code snippets.

**Initial Assessment: Potential Time Zone Shenanigans**

WHOA! Right off the bat, I see a pattern emerging. That `.local-time-value` CSS selector appearing in multiple stylesheets – `trays.css`, `cards.css`, and `card-columns.css` – screams "time-related styling" to me. That's immediately triggering alarm bells because inconsistent or improper time zone handling is a classic source of bugs, especially in web applications that deal with users in different time zones.

Then I see the `include TimeHelper` in `app/models/user/day_timeline/column.rb` and, even better, the empty `app/helpers/time_helper.rb` file. This tells me we *might* have some custom time formatting or manipulation happening, but the empty file leaves me *wanting* more information.

**Diving Deeper: Comprehensive Audit Required**

My immediate next step is clear. I need to conduct a thorough investigation. I'm going to meticulously inspect every single view that renders dates or times. This means digging through the `.erb` files within `app/views/` (and being sure to skip JSON and Jbuilder templates). I'm also going to pay close attention to any JavaScript files, like `bubble_controller.js`, to see how dates and times are handled on the client-side. CSS files are on the list as well!

And *while* I'm searching I'm going to filter my search in `app/views/` to make sure nothing is excluded from the results.

This is going to be a deep dive. I'm looking for clues about:

*   How are dates and times being formatted for display?
*   Is the application aware of user time zones?
*   Are there any conversions happening between different time zones (e.g., UTC, local time)?
*   Are there any potential areas where time zone information might be lost or misinterpreted?
*   Is there any use of `local-time-value` in javascript?

I need a complete picture to assess the current state of time zone management in this codebase and identify any potential issues before they become real problems.

class User::DayTimeline
  include Serializable

  attr_reader :user, :day, :filter

  delegate :today?, to: :day

  def initialize(user, day, filter)
    @user, @day, @filter = user, day, filter
  end

  def has_activity?
    events.any?
  end

  def events
    filtered_events.where(created_at: window).order(created_at: :desc)
  end

  def next_day
    latest_event_before&.created_at
  end

  def earliest_time
    next_day&.tomorrow&.beginning_of_day
  end

  def latest_time
    day.yesterday.beginning_of_day
  end

  def added_column
    @added_column ||= build_column(:added, "Added", 1, events.where(action: %w[card_published card_reopened]))
  end

  def updated_column
    @updated_column ||= build_column(:updated, "Updated", 2, events.where.not(action: %w[card_published card_closed card_reopened]))
  end

  def closed_column
    @closed_column ||= build_column(:closed, "Done", 3, events.where(action: "card_closed"))
  end

  def cache_key
    ActiveSupport::Cache.expand_cache_key [ user, filter, day.to_date, Time.zone.name, events ], "day-timeline"
  end

  private
    TIMELINEABLE_ACTIONS = %w[
      card_assigned
      card_unassigned
      card_published
      card_closed
      card_reopened
      card_collection_changed
      card_board_changed
      card_postponed
      card_auto_postponed
      card_triaged
      card_sent_back_to_triage
      comment_created
    ]

    def filtered_events
      @filtered_events ||= begin
        events = timelineable_events
        events = events.where(creator_id: filter.creators.ids) if filter.creators.present?
        events
      end
    end

    def timelineable_events
      Event
        .preloaded
        .where(board: boards)
        .where(action: TIMELINEABLE_ACTIONS)
    end

    def boards
      filter.boards.presence || user.boards
    end

    def latest_event_before
      filtered_events.where(created_at: ...day.beginning_of_day).chronologically.last
    end

    def build_column(id, base_title, index, events)
      Column.new(self, id, base_title, index, events)
    end

    def window
      day.all_day
    end
end

class User::DayTimeline::Column
  include ActionView::Helpers::TagHelper, ActionView::Helpers::OutputSafetyHelper, TimeHelper

  attr_reader :index, :id, :base_title, :day_timeline, :events

  def initialize(day_timeline, id, base_title, index, events)
    @id = id
    @day_timeline = day_timeline
    @base_title = base_title
    @index = index
    @events = events
  end

  def title
    date_tag = tag.span day_timeline.day.strftime("%A, %B %-d")
    parts = [ base_title, date_tag ]
    parts << tag.span("(#{full_events_count})", class: "font-weight-normal") if full_events_count > 0
    safe_join(parts, " ")
  end

  def events_by_hour
    limited_events.group_by { it.created_at.hour }
  end

  def has_more_events?
    limited_events.count < full_events_count
  end

  def hidden_events_count
    full_events_count - limited_events.count
  end

  def to_param
    id
  end

  private
    def limited_events
      @limited_events ||= events.limit(100).load
    end

    def full_events_count
      @full_events_count ||= events.count
    end
end

Okay, here's what I'm thinking, connecting all these dots... We've got a serious time rendering inconsistency issue. My initial thought process focused on the code, and how seemingly small things can have big consequences.

First off, I notice that the `comments.css:177` file's `.comment__permalink-title` and `app/views/events/_empty_days.html.erb` both use capitalization methods. They capitalize dates like "today" or "yesterday", which looks sloppy. That's a good place to start.

Then I realized, it's not just capitalization; it's the *way* dates and times are being formatted and how they’re displayed with respect to the client's timezone versus the server's timezone, which is the crux of the problem. We've got timestamps all over the place: in the card closures, the card meta data updates, the comments, the notifications... every single one of these instances is a potential problem. We are baking the server's timezone into these rendered elements, which the problem statement explicitly says we *don't* want!

It's clear that we need to stop rendering dates on the server-side! We need to move the responsibility to the client-side. The server should only be sending raw timestamps.

class TimeWindowParser
  attr_reader :now

  HUMAN_NAMES_BY_VALUE = {
    "today" => "Today",
    "yesterday" => "Yesterday",
    "thisweek" => "This week",
    "thismonth" => "This month",
    "thisyear" => "This year",
    "lastweek" => "Last week",
    "lastmonth" => "Last month",
    "lastyear" => "Last year"
  }

  VALUES = HUMAN_NAMES_BY_VALUE.keys

  class << self
    def parse(string)
      new.parse(string)
    end

    def human_name_for(value)
      HUMAN_NAMES_BY_VALUE[value]
    end
  end

  def initialize(now: Time.current)
    @now = now
  end

  def parse(string)
    case normalize(string)
    when "today"
      now.all_day
    when "yesterday"
      (now - 1.day).all_day
    when "thisweek"
      now.all_week
    when "thismonth"
      now.all_month
    when "thisyear"
      now.all_year
    when "lastweek"
      (now - 1.week).all_week
    when "lastmonth"
      (now - 1.month).all_month
    when "lastyear"
      (now - 1.year).all_year
    end
  end

  private
    def normalize(string)
      if string
        string.downcase.gsub(/[\s_\-]/, "")
      end
    end
end

First possibility: if `data-controller="local-time"` is attached to the `<body>` tag in both `application.html.erb` and `public.html.erb`, I think I can make a plan.

I should be able to make use of `data-action="turbo:morph@document->local-time#refreshAll"`. Alternatively, I could add event listeners directly in the `connect()` method for events like `turbo:morph`, `turbo:frame-render`, and potentially `visibilitychange`. I need to remember `turbo:frame-render` already triggers `targetConnected` for new elements, and `turbo:morph` fires on `document` after every morph, and `turbo:morph-element` fires when a single frame morphs such as when using `refresh: :morph` on a `turbo-frame`.

Now, what happens with `turbo:morph-element` on a `<turbo-frame refresh="morph">`? I need to check. When a `<turbo-frame refresh="morph">` refreshes, does it fire `turbo:morph` or `turbo:morph-element`? I need to look into this more deeply.

It triggers `turbo:before-morph-element` and `turbo:morph-element` *which bubbles!* on the morphed elements, and `turbo:frame-render` on the `<turbo-frame>` which *also bubbles!* And when a full-page morph happens, Turbo fires `turbo:morph` on the `document` *and* `turbo:morph-element` on the morphed elements!

Okay, so in the `local_time_controller.js`, I should design for the following.

*   Handle `*TargetConnected(target)` and immediately format the target!
*   Listen to `turbo:morph@document`, `turbo:morph-element` and `turbo:before-cache`. For `turbo:before-cache`, keeping the formatted text would mean Turbo cache previews don't flash blank, and on restore `connect()`/`refreshAll()` immediately updates it!
*   Listen to `turbo:morph` on `document` to call `#refreshAll()`!
*   Listen to `turbo:frame-render` on `document` to call `#refreshAll()` in case a frame morphed in place with `refresh="morph"`!
*   Have a periodic `setInterval` (e.g. every 30s or 60s) *and* `visibilitychange` (for when a tab becomes visible again after sleeping overnight!) to also call `#refreshAll()`!

Wait, what about `turbo:before-morph-element`? The library Idiomorph can see something like `<time datetime="2025-09-12T10:00:00Z" data-local-time-target="agooron">yesterday</time>` and replace it with `<time datetime="2025-09-12T10:00:00Z" data-local-time-target="agooron"></time>`, Idiomorph would wipe `"yesterday"` to `""` before `turbo:morph` runs which should be synchronously so no flicker!

module Card::Entropic
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    scope :postponing_soon, -> do
      now = Time.now
      active
        .joins(board: :account)
        .left_outer_joins(board: :entropy)
        .joins("LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies AS account_entropies ON account_entropies.account_id = accounts.id AND account_entropies.container_type = 'Account' AND account_entropies.container_id = accounts.id")
        .where("last_active_at > #{connection.date_subtract('?', 'COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)')}", now)
        .where("last_active_at <= #{connection.date_subtract('?', 'COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period) * 0.75')}", now)
    end

    delegate :auto_postpone_period, to: :board
  end

  class_methods do
    # Iterates per account, grouping the account's boards by their effective
    # auto-postpone period (board override, else account default). Each group
    # queries with a single constant cutoff, so `account_id = ? AND
    # last_active_at <= ?` rides the existing index instead of computing the
    # threshold per row across every card in the system.
    def auto_postpone_all_due(as_of: Time.now)
      Account.find_each do |account|
        account.boards.includes(:entropy).group_by(&:auto_postpone_period).each do |period, boards|
          account.cards.active
            .where(board_id: boards.map(&:id))
            .where(last_active_at: ..(as_of - period))
            .find_each do |card|
              card.auto_postpone(user: account.system_user)
            end
        end
      end
    end
  end

  def entropy
    Card::Entropy.for(self)
  end

  def entropic?
    entropy.present?
  end
end

**Deep Dive into Hotwire Native Bridge Attributes and Timezones**

Okay, let's break this down. My goal here is to eliminate server-side date formatting within the cached HTML of Hotwire Native Bridge components, specifically within the `bridge_helper.rb` and associated JavaScript controllers. I'm focusing on `bridge_helper.rb`, `bridge/stamp_controller.js`, and `bridge/share_controller.js`.

The current approach in `_stamp.html.erb` bakes server-side formatted dates into the cached HTML: `card.postponed_at.strftime("%b %d, %Y")`.  This is a huge no-no, right? We need to push this formatting to the client for timezone-awareness. The key is the interaction between the Ruby view and the JavaScript controller.

I'm thinking:

1.  **For the Stamp Controller:**  Instead of `bridge_description: card.postponed_at.strftime("%b %d, %Y")`, which commits to a specific format and timezone, we can use a pure ISO-8601 timestamp in the HTML itself. For instance, `data-bridge-description-datetime="2025-09-12T17:42:00Z"`. The `stamp_controller.js` will read this attribute, and using a date formatting helper, can then render this into the viewers timezone. The `stamp_controller.js` could even fall back to the existing `bridge_description` attribute if one is provided. The use of a mutation observer in `stamp_controller.js` gives us the flexibility to update the UI on the client.

2.  **For the Share Controller:**  The function `bridge_share_card_description(card)` formats dates. I can move this formatting to the browser in a similar way:  pass ISO timestamps (like `card.created_at.utc.iso8601`) or data attributes (`data-bridge-share-added-at`, `data-bridge-share-updated-at`) into the HTML and let `share_controller.js` handle formatting. I can even pass this as a template with placeholders like `{{added_at}}` / `{{updated_at}}` and replace them.

Basically, I want to centralize the date formatting logic in a shared JavaScript helper module, which can be reused across both controllers. This ensures consistency and prevents server-side date calculations from being cached in the HTML. messages.thinking:
**My Analysis of Time and Date Rendering in Fizzy**

Okay, here's what I've been thinking about, boiling this down to the core. I see a *lot* of time-related calls, particularly in the views with those `fresh_when` and `<% cache ... do %>` fragments. These are *prime* targets for improvement, and it's clear there's some timezone baked-in caching going on that's not ideal, with server timezones being stored in fragments. It needs a massive overhaul.

I've taken a deep dive, and the core of the problem stems from the rendering of dates and times *everywhere*.  The existing code pre-computes these values with timezone, then bakes them into the cache, and the result is the viewer's *local* timezone isn't accounted for. This is where it breaks down.

I've identified these key things:

1.  **Multiple Caching Issues:** There are instances where time-related elements are cached, but they are not user-specific, leading to timezone discrepancies. This is especially true for shared elements like comments and notifications.  There are a lot of these in several view fragments, I've got a list.

2.  **Date/Time Formatting inconsistencies:** The app has a handful of different time and date formatting styles and they render differently across the application.  Some use `strftime`, which is not ideal when trying to render in the client's local timezone.

3.  **The Prompt:** The prompt wants dates and times in the viewer's own timezone.

4.  **The Fix:** I can fix *everything* in a single controller. `local_time_controller.js` to render dates/times in the browser. I can move the logic for formatting time and dates there to be calculated, then display the correct information.

**My Solution**

Here's my design for the controller.  I've distilled it into a minimal set of styles that can handle every use case:

1.  `time` (Time of Day): "1:42 PM" (short local time). Uses `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { timeStyle: "short" })`.  I'm going to normalize any no-break spaces to regular spaces because ICU sometimes does that. This will match the prompt and the current format already being used.

2.  `date` (Calendar Date): "Sep 12, 2025".  Uses `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { month: "short", day: "numeric", year: "numeric" })`. Will work for those card stamps that are already using this format.

3.  `datetime` (Date and Time): "Sep 12, 2025, 1:42 PM". Uses `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { month: "short", day: "numeric", year: "numeric", hour: "numeric", minute: "2-digit" })`. I'll use this for full timestamps in tables.

4.  `indays` (Calendar Day, "Today", "Yesterday", "Monday, September 12"): This gets a little more complex. I want to use this for the calendar headers.  This is based on the calendar difference.  If it's the same day, I'll use "today". If it's yesterday, I'll use "yesterday", etc. Otherwise it will be the full day with name, month, etc. This is needed for day headers in the events timelines.

5.  `agooron` (Relative Time with Prepositions): "at 1:42 PM", "yesterday", "5 days ago", "on Sep 5", "on Sep 12, 2024".  This is the *core* style for the "added/updated" type stamps. This also needs to handle future dates. The output format depends on the difference between the current date and the given timestamp, matching the natural language used in the app. For example, "added at 1:42 PM", "completed by Kevin yesterday", "Added on Sep 5". It will be wrapped with `<span class="local-time-value">` so styles are consistent.

6. `relative` (Relative Time): Short relative time like `"1:42 PM"`, `"yesterday"`, `"5 days ago"`, `"Sep 12"`, `"Sep 12, 2024"`. If it's a day, render just the day, not a full timestamp. If it's a month, it will render `Sep 12`. If it's last year, render `Sep 12, 2024`.

7.

messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive: Conquering Dynamic DOM Updates in Fizzy**

Okay, let's break this down. The `title_controller.js` is totally decoupled and unaffected – it's just observing the intersection of the `headerTarget`, so we can put that aside. I'm focusing on the `local-time` controller and ensuring it handles *every* edge case related to dynamic DOM updates.

First, the initial page load is straightforward. Stimulus handles connecting and formatting all `<time>` targets. Turbo Drive navigations are also manageable. The controller disconnects on the old body and reconnects on the new, re-formatting everything. Similarly, Turbo Drive previews from cache restore a previous state, and a connection and re-format handles things.

Turbo Frame loads and Turbo Streams present new elements. Stimulus' MutationObserver does its job, and target connections happen naturally, triggering updates. No issues there.

Now, Turbo Morph is where things get interesting and complicated. This is the critical edge case. Idiomorph might remove the internal content of the `<time>` element during a morph, even if the element itself stays put. Crucially, *this means Stimulus' `targetConnected` isn't triggered*. So how do we handle this gracefully?

The solution lies in leveraging Turbo's lifecycle events. I'm going to listen for `turbo:morph` on the `document` – this allows a full refresh when an entire page is morphed. Also, `turbo:morph-element` is dispatched for *every* morphed element, even if content isn't changed. And, `turbo:frame-render` will trigger as well. If the target of this event is a `[data-local-time-target]` or contains one, I can refresh it or them, guaranteeing consistency. Listening to `visibilitychange` will help with background tab scenarios.

Then, there's the periodic timer that is important. I need to make sure I schedule a refresh on an interval, like every 60 seconds, to handle time changes, especially when timezones might change. We can't rely on `*TargetConnected` alone.

Crucially, on `disconnect`, I'll need to clean up my event listeners and the `setInterval`. I think using an `AbortController` will be the cleanest approach for managing those listeners. I'll need to check if that approach is used in other Fizzy controllers.

Even better, even if a `<time>` element's `datetime` attribute *doesn't* change during a morph, `turbo:morph-element` will still fire. So, whether the timestamp is updated or not, my `turbo:morph-element` handler will synchronously re-format the element after Idiomorph does its thing. So, no flicker and complete correctness! I need to verify that Turbo dispatches these events as I expect in the installed version of `@hotwired/turbo-rails` (and check how other Fizzy controllers use them).

  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

    has_one :not_now, dependent: :destroy, class_name: "Card::NotNow"

  end

module Card::Postponable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_one :not_now, dependent: :destroy, class_name: "Card::NotNow"

    scope :postponed, -> { open.published.joins(:not_now) }
    scope :active, -> { open.published.where.missing(:not_now) }
  end

  def postponed?
    open? && published? && not_now.present?
  end

  def postponed_at
    not_now&.created_at
  end

  def postponed_by
    not_now&.user
  end

  def active?
    open? && published? && !postponed?
  end

  def auto_postpone(**args)
    postpone(**args, event_name: :auto_postponed)
  end

  def postpone(user: Current.user, event_name: :postponed)
    transaction do
      send_back_to_triage(skip_event: true)
      reopen
      activity_spike&.destroy
      create_not_now!(user: user) unless postponed?
      track_event event_name, creator: user
    end
  end

  def resume
    transaction do
      reopen
      activity_spike&.destroy
      not_now&.destroy
    end
  end
end

module Card::Closeable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_one :closure, dependent: :destroy

    scope :closed, -> { joins(:closure) }
    scope :open, -> { where.missing(:closure) }

    scope :recently_closed_first, -> { closed.order(closures: { created_at: :desc }) }
    scope :closed_at_window, ->(window) { closed.where(closures: { created_at: window }) }
    scope :closed_by, ->(users) { closed.where(closures: { user_id: Array(users) }) }
  end

  def closed?
    closure.present?
  end

  def open?
    !closed?
  end

  def closed_by
    closure&.user
  end

  def closed_at
    closure&.created_at
  end

  def close(user: Current.user)
    unless closed?
      transaction do
        not_now&.destroy
        create_closure! user: user
        track_event :closed, creator: user
      end
    end
  end

  def reopen(user: Current.user)
    if closed?
      transaction do
        closure&.destroy
        track_event :reopened, creator: user
      end
    end
  end
end

messages.content: Let's reproduce the issue with `bin/rails runner` by inspecting the rendered HTML of a comment and card under two different timezones (`America/New_York` vs `Asia/Tokyo`).
messages.thinking:
Okay, here's what I'm thinking:

**Thoroughly Reviewed and Verified Timezone Concerns**

Alright, every potential source of timezone-related bugs has been accounted for, and I've double-checked every view and helper. I can confirm that there aren't any sneaky issues. Specifically:

1.  **Email Templates:** `app/views/mailers/**/*` are safe. No JavaScript in the emails, and the `Notification::Bundle#deliver` method specifically uses `user.in_time_zone` to handle any time-related conversions.
2.  **Magic Link Expiration:** `app/views/sessions/magic_links/show.html.erb:18` uses `distance_of_time_in_words(MagicLink::EXPIRATION_TIME)`. However, the `MagicLink::EXPIRATION_TIME` is a constant value representing a duration ("15 minutes") and not a timestamp.
3.  **Date Formatting for IDs/URLs:** The use of `strftime("%Y-%m-%d")` in `app/helpers/pagination_helper.rb`, `app/views/users/events/show.html.erb`, and `app/views/users/_activity_timeline.html.erb` is intentionally for things like URL query parameters (`day=`) and DOM `id` attributes. This formatting is **not** used for displaying dates or times to users, so this is not where the problem resides.

Now, before I start making changes, I need to reproduce the problematic behavior *exactly* as it is now. This is crucial for verifying that the fixes work as intended.

Based on my current understanding:
1.  **Caching Timezone Dependent Strings:** The core issue appears to be that time zone-dependent strings like `"Monday, May 12, 1:42 PM"`, `"Sep 12, 2025"`, and `"2 minutes ago"` are being baked directly into the HTML within the fragment cache (`<% cache comment %>`, `<% cache card %>`, etc.) in files like `app/views/cards/comments/_comment.html.erb`, `app/views/cards/display/common/_meta.html.erb`, `app/views/cards/display/common/_stamp.html.erb`, and `app/views/notifications/notification/_header.html.erb`. This means if a user in New York warms the cache, a user in Tokyo will get the New York time baked into the fragment. Also, the `"2 minutes ago"` format will stay permanently as `"2 minutes ago"` in the cache.

I'll use `bin/rails runner` to create a reproduction command. This will allow me to check the HTML output for a comment, card, closure notice and a notification from two different server timezones, without modifying any code yet. That should allow me to verify the exact problematic behavior first.

arguments.command:
bin/rails runner '
  account = Account.first
  Current.with_account(account) do
    user = account.users.active.first
    Current.session = user.identity.sessions.create!(user_agent: "test", ip_address: "127.0.0.1")
    comment = Comment.first
    card = comment.card

    ["America/New_York", "Asia/Tokyo"].each do |tz|
      Time.use_zone(tz) do
        html = ApplicationController.render(partial: "cards/comments/comment", locals: { comment: comment })
        puts "=== Comment in #{tz} ==="
        puts html[/<a[^>]*comment__permalink-title.*?<\/a>/m]
      end
    end

    card_html = ApplicationController.render(partial: "cards/display/common/meta", locals: { card: card })
    puts "=== Card meta ==="
    puts card_html[/card__meta-text--added.*?<\/span>/m]
    puts card_html[/card__meta-text--updated.*?<\/span>/m]
  end
'

    begin

      # Format: 48-bit timestamp_ms | 12-bit sub_ms_precision | 4-bit version | 62-bit random

      time_ms = time.to_f * 1000
      timestamp_ms = time_ms.to_i

      # 48-bit timestamp (milliseconds since epoch)
      bytes = []
      bytes[0] = (timestamp_ms >> 40) & 0xff
      bytes[1] = (timestamp_ms >> 32) & 0xff
      bytes[2] = (timestamp_ms >> 24) & 0xff
      bytes[3] = (timestamp_ms >> 16) & 0xff
      bytes[4] = (timestamp_ms >> 8) & 0xff

      # Extract fractional milliseconds and convert to 12-bit value (0-4095)

      bytes[6] = ((sub_ms_precision >> 8) & 0x0f) | 0x70  # version 7
      bytes[7] = sub_ms_precision & 0xff

require "test_helper"

class TimeHelperTest < ActionView::TestCase
  test "local_datetime_tag emits an empty time element with UTC ISO-8601 datetime" do
    time = Time.utc(2025, 9, 12, 17, 42, 0)

    html = local_datetime_tag(time)

    assert_equal %(<time datetime="2025-09-12T17:42:00Z" data-local-time-target="time"></time>), html
  end

  test "local_datetime_tag emits identical HTML regardless of server timezone" do
    utc_time = Time.utc(2025, 9, 12, 17, 42, 0)

    ny_html = Time.use_zone("America/New_York") { local_datetime_tag(utc_time.in_time_zone, style: :relative) }
    tokyo_html = Time.use_zone("Asia/Tokyo") { local_datetime_tag(utc_time.in_time_zone, style: :relative) }

    assert_equal ny_html, tokyo_html
    assert_equal %(<time datetime="2025-09-12T17:42:00Z" data-local-time-target="relative"></time>), ny_html
  end

  test "local_datetime_tag merges additional attributes and data attributes" do
    time = Time.utc(2025, 9, 12, 17, 42, 0)

    html = local_datetime_tag(time, style: :agooron, class: "custom", data: { test: "value" })
    fragment = Nokogiri::HTML::DocumentFragment.parse(html)
    time_element = fragment.at_css("time")

    assert_equal "2025-09-12T17:42:00Z", time_element["datetime"]
    assert_equal "agooron", time_element["data-local-time-target"]
    assert_equal "value", time_element["data-test"]
    assert_equal "custom", time_element["class"]
    assert_equal "", time_element.text
  end
end
EOF

    assert_select "time[datetime='#{cards(:logo).last_active_at.utc.iso8601}'][data-local-time-target='agooron']", text: ""
  end

  test "card show sends raw UTC timestamps for meta, comments, and auto-close notice" do
    card = cards(:logo)

    get card_path(card)
    assert_response :success

    assert_select ".card__meta-text--added time[datetime='#{card.created_at.utc.iso8601}'][data-local-time-target='agooron']", text: ""
    assert_select ".card__meta-text--updated time[datetime='#{card.last_active_at.utc.iso8601}'][data-local-time-target='agooron']", text: ""
    assert_select "##{dom_id(comment)} .comment__permalink-title time[datetime='#{comment.created_at.utc.iso8601}'][data-local-time-target='relative']", text: ""
    assert_select "##{dom_id(card, :closure_notice)} time[datetime='#{card.entropy.auto_clean_at.utc.iso8601}'][data-local-time-target='indays']", text: ""
  end

  test "closed and postponed cards send raw UTC timestamps for stamps and closure notice" do
    closed_card = cards(:shipping)
    get card_path(closed_card)
    assert_response :success

    assert_select ".card__closed[data-bridge-description-datetime='#{closed_card.closed_at.utc.iso8601}']"
    assert_select ".card__closed-date time[datetime='#{closed_card.closed_at.utc.iso8601}'][data-local-time-target='date']", text: ""
    assert_select ".card-perma__closure-message time[datetime='#{closed_card.closed_at.utc.iso8601}'][data-local-time-target='agooron']", text: ""

    postponed_card.postpone(user: users(:kevin))
    get card_path(postponed_card)
    assert_response :success

    assert_select ".card__closed[data-bridge-description-datetime='#{postponed_card.postponed_at.utc.iso8601}']"
    assert_select ".card__closed-date time[datetime='#{postponed_card.postponed_at.utc.iso8601}'][data-local-time-target='date']", text: ""
  end

      assert_response :success

      get card_path(card)

1.  **Leverage Real Timestamps and CDP**: I'll use real timestamps, relative to `Time.current`, and compute the expected local strings in Ruby using `ActiveSupport::TimeZone[tz]`. Critically, I'll use CDP's `Emulation.setTimezoneOverride` to test both `America/New_York` and `Asia/Tokyo`.
2.  **Deterministic Test Cases**: For specific clock-dependent scenarios (like "2 hours ago," "yesterday," "5 days ago," DST changes, etc.), I'll calculate precise timestamps relative to `Time.current` in the overridden browser timezone. For instance, to avoid flakiness:

    *   I'll employ similar strategies for all the other time ranges, accounting for the possibility of cross-day scenarios and ensuring predictable results.
3.  **Explicit Clock Control**: For exact timing scenarios, I can pass a specific `now` timestamp to the ES module `"helpers/time_helpers"` within Chromium using `page.evaluate_async_script`.     set_browser_timezone("America/New_York")

    today_time = now.hour >= 2 ? (now - 2.hours).change(sec: 0) : now.beginning_of_day + 5.minutes
    last_night = now.yesterday.end_of_day - 30.minutes
    five_days_ago = now - 5.days
    earlier_this_year = now.yday > 14 ? (now - 14.days) : (now + 14.days)
    last_year = (now - 400.days).change(hour: 13, min: 42, sec: 0)

    card = cards(:logo)
    card.update_columns(created_at: five_days_ago, last_active_at: (now.tomorrow.beginning_of_day + 1.hour) - card.auto_postpone_period)

    c_yesterday = card.comments.create!(creator: users(:kevin), body: "Last night comment", created_at: last_night)

require "application_system_test_case"

class LocalTimeTest < ApplicationSystemTestCase
  setup do
    using_wait_time(10) { sign_in_as users(:kevin) }
  end

  teardown do
    set_browser_timezone("")
  end

  test "comments, card meta, auto-close notice, stamps, and access tokens render in the viewer's own timezone" do
    set_browser_timezone("America/New_York")
    tz = ActiveSupport::TimeZone["America/New_York"]
    now = Time.current.in_time_zone(tz)

    today_time = now.hour >= 2 ? (now - 2.hours).change(sec: 0) : now.beginning_of_day + 5.minutes
    last_night = now.yesterday.end_of_day - 30.minutes
    five_days_ago = now - 5.days
    earlier_this_year = now.yday > 14 ? (now - 14.days) : (now + 14.days)
    last_year = (now - 400.days).change(hour: 13, min: 42, sec: 0)

    card = cards(:logo)
    c_today = card.comments.create!(creator: users(:kevin), body: "Today comment", created_at: today_time)
    c_yesterday = card.comments.create!(creator: users(:kevin), body: "Last night comment", created_at: last_night)
    c_five_days = card.comments.create!(creator: users(:kevin), body: "Earlier in week comment", created_at: five_days_ago)
    c_older_same_year = card.comments.create!(creator: users(:kevin), body: "Older same year comment", created_at: earlier_this_year)
    c_last_year = card.comments.create!(creator: users(:kevin), body: "Last year comment", created_at: last_year)

    card.update_columns(created_at: five_days_ago, last_active_at: (now.tomorrow.beginning_of_day + 1.hour) - card.auto_postpone_period)

    visit card_url(card)

    # Comment timestamps
    assert_time_text "##{dom_id(c_today)} .comment__permalink-title time", today_time.strftime("%-l:%M %p")
    assert_time_text "##{dom_id(c_yesterday)} .comment__permalink-title time", "yesterday"
    assert_time_text "##{dom_id(c_five_days)} .comment__permalink-title time", "5 days ago"
    assert_time_text "##{dom_id(c_older_same_year)} .comment__permalink-title time", earlier_this_year.strftime("%b %-d")
    assert_time_text "##{dom_id(c_last_year)} .comment__permalink-title time", last_year.strftime("%b %-d, %Y")

    # Tooltip contains full localized date & time
    assert_includes find("##{dom_id(c_today)} .comment__permalink-title time")[:title], today_time.strftime("%-l:%M %p")

    # Card meta uses .local-time-value span
    assert_time_text ".card__meta-text--added time", "5 days ago"
    assert_selector ".card__meta-text--added time .local-time-value"

    # Card auto-closing overnight -> "tomorrow" (and entropy bubble agrees: Closes in 1 day)
    assert_selector "##{dom_id(card, :closure_notice)}", text: /Moves to “Not Now” tomorrow if there’s no activity\./
    assert_selector "##{dom_id(card, :bubble)} [data-bubble-target='center']", text: "1"

    # Card auto-closing in 3 days -> "in 3 days" (and entropy bubble agrees: Closes in 3 days)
    card.update_column(:last_active_at, (now + 3.days) - card.auto_postpone_period)
    visit card_url(card)
    assert_selector "##{dom_id(card, :closure_notice)}", text: /Moves to “Not Now” in 3 days if there’s no activity\./
    assert_selector "##{dom_id(card, :bubble)} [data-bubble-target='center']", text: "3"

    # Card auto-closing later today -> "today"
    card.update_column(:last_active_at, (now.end_of_day - 5.minutes) - card.auto_postpone_period)
    visit card_url(card)
    assert_selector "##{dom_id(card, :closure_notice)}", text: /Moves to “Not Now” today if there’s no activity\./

    # Posting a new comment via Turbo Stream renders its local time immediately
    fill_in_lexxy with: "Fresh live comment"
    click_on "Post"
    assert_selector ".comment", text: "Fresh live comment"
    live_comment = card.comments.order(:created_at).last
    assert_selector "##{dom_id(live_comment)} .comment__permalink-title time .local-time-value", text: /\A\d{1,2}:\d{2} [AP]M\z/

    # Closed card stamp and closure message
    closed_card = cards(:shipping)
    closed_at = Time.utc(2025, 9, 12, 17, 42, 0) # Sep 12 1:42 PM in NY, Sep 13 2:42 AM in Tokyo
    closed_card.closure.update_column(:created_at, closed_at)

    visit card_url(closed_card)
    assert_time_text ".card__closed-date time", "Sep 12, 2025"
    assert_time_text ".card-perma__closure-message time", "on Sep 12, 2025"

    # Switch browser to Asia/Tokyo — the EXACT same UTC timestamp flips to Sep 13, 2025!
    set_browser_timezone("Asia/Tokyo")
    visit card_url(closed_card)
    assert_time_text ".card__closed-date time", "Sep 13, 2025"
    assert_time_text ".card-perma__closure-message time", "on Sep 13, 2025"

    # Access tokens table renders full date and time in viewer's timezone
    token = identities(:kevin).access_tokens.create!(description: "CLI token", permission: "read")
    token.update_column(:created_at, closed_at)

    set_browser_timezone("America/New_York")
